common_name: Carol Mountain Laurel (Tall Red-Budded White-Flowered Selection)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Carol is a vigorous, taller-growing mountain laurel noted for abundant bright red buds opening to near-white flowers.

directions: Site in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, where mountain laurel performs best, though Carol also tolerates considerable sun in cooler climates or with consistent moisture. In mid to late spring, dense clusters of vivid red buds open to pure white flowers sometimes lightly blushed pink, set against compact, glossy, slightly twisted evergreen foliage. A strong, upright grower reaching 6 to 10 feet tall and as wide at maturity, Carol naturalizes well and makes an effective specimen, informal hedge, or woodland-edge foundation planting. Prune lightly just after flowering if shaping is needed, since next year's buds form soon after bloom, and keep in mind that all parts of the plant are toxic if ingested.
sources: Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station (Richard Jaynes Kalmia breeding program)

common_name: Berry Heavy Winterberry Holly (Vigorous Heavy-Fruiting Female Winterberry)

planting.note: Plant female shrubs alongside a compatible male pollinator such as Mr. Poppins or Jim Dandy in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to part shade; Berry Heavy is a Proven Winners selection prized for an unusually dense, heavy berry set.

directions: Plant in moist to wet, acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to part shade, siting a compatible male pollinator such as Mr. Poppins or Jim Dandy within roughly 50 feet, since winterberry is dioecious and female plants need a nearby male to set fruit. Berry Heavy produces an exceptionally dense, heavy crop of bright red berries that coat the bare branches from fall through winter, on a full-sized, well-branched shrub that tolerates wet, boggy soils better than most woody landscape plants. Its reliable, abundant fruit display is a favorite for winter arrangements and for sustaining overwintering songbirds through the cold months. Prune only lightly and only after flowering, since flower buds form on the previous year's wood.

common_name: Berry Heavy Gold Winterberry Holly (Gold-Fruited Sport of Berry Heavy)

planting.note: Plant female shrubs alongside a compatible male pollinator such as Mr. Poppins or Jim Dandy in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to part shade; Berry Heavy Gold is a chance-seedling sport bearing the largest, brightest gold fruit among winterberry cultivars.

directions: Plant in moist to wet, acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to part shade, siting a compatible male pollinator such as Mr. Poppins or Jim Dandy within roughly 50 feet, since this all-female selection needs a nearby male to set fruit. Originally found as a chance yellow-berried seedling, Berry Heavy Gold bears unusually large, luminous golden-yellow fruit in heavy clusters that persist on bare branches well into winter, offering a striking alternative to the more common red-berried winterberry cultivars. Its upright, mounded habit and slow, dense growth make it a strong anchor for a mixed winter-interest border, and its fruit holds color and size better than most other gold-berried selections on the market. Prune only lightly and only after flowering, since flower buds form on the previous year's wood.

common_name: Berry Poppins Winterberry Holly (Compact Dwarf Heavy-Fruiting Female Winterberry)

planting.note: Plant female shrubs alongside the compact male pollinator Mr. Poppins in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to part shade; Berry Poppins is a true dwarf Proven Winners winterberry bred for small-space gardens.

directions: Plant in moist to wet, acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to part shade, siting the male pollinator Mr. Poppins within roughly 50 feet, since this dwarf female needs a nearby male to set fruit. Berry Poppins tops out at just 3 to 4 feet tall and wide, a fraction of the 6-to-10-foot size of wild winterberry, yet still produces an abundant, heavier-than-average crop of bright red berries that light up the bare branches in fall and winter. Its true dwarf habit makes it a rare fit for foundation plantings, small gardens, and rain gardens where full-sized winterberry cultivars would overwhelm the space. Prune only lightly and only after flowering, since flower buds form on the previous year's wood.

common_name: Mr. Poppins Winterberry Holly (Compact Dwarf Male Pollinator)

planting.note: Plant as a non-fruiting male pollinator within about 50 feet of dwarf female winterberry cultivars such as Berry Poppins, Berry Heavy, or Berry Heavy Gold in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to part shade.

directions: Plant in moist to wet, acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to part shade, within roughly 50 feet of the female winterberry cultivars it is meant to pollinate, since winterberry is dioecious and depends on a nearby male for fruit set. Mr. Poppins was bred specifically as a space-saving dwarf counterpart to Proven Winners' compact female selections, staying at just 3 to 4 feet tall and wide instead of the much larger males typically paired with full-sized winterberry. It bears small white flowers in late spring that provide pollen but no berries of its own, and one plant can pollinate up to five females sited within range. Because it offers little seasonal color on its own, tuck Mr. Poppins into a less prominent spot in the landscape and let its female companions carry the winter display.
